languages.label: Python
languages.tagline: Runtime semantics, stdlib, and the sharp edges.

misconceptions.description: int() on a negative float rounds down (toward negative infinity) rather than truncating toward zero, so int(-3.9) is believed to be -4.
Believing float('nan') == float('nan') is True; NaN is never equal to anything, including itself.
Believing / performs integer division when both operands are ints, so 7 / 2 gives 3 instead of the float 3.5.
Believing the % operator takes the sign of the dividend as in C, so -7 % 3 is -1 rather than 2 (Python's result takes the divisor's sign).
Believing -2 ** 2 equals 4 because unary minus is applied before **; actually ** binds tighter, giving -4.
Believing 1 < 2 < 3 is evaluated as (1 < 2) < 3 rather than as (1 < 2) and (2 < 3).
Believing and/or always return True or False, rather than returning one of their operands, so 3 or 5 is thought to be True.
Believing bool is unrelated to int, so True == 1 is False or errors; in fact bool subclasses int.
Believing == None and is None are always equivalent, ignoring that a custom __eq__ can change the result of == None.
Believing isinstance takes several types as separate arguments or a list, rather than a single tuple of types.
Believing tuples and strings support item assignment like lists, so t[0] = 5 or s[0] = 'H' succeeds.
Believing a slice with an out-of-range bound raises IndexError, when slices silently clamp to the sequence's ends.
Believing the stop index of a slice is inclusive, so [1:3] includes the element at index 3.
Believing [[]] * 3 creates three independent inner lists, when it repeats references to the same list.
Believing a = b = c = [] gives three separate lists rather than three names bound to one list.
Believing list2 = list1 copies the list, so mutating list2 won't affect list1.
Believing lst[:] returns a reference to the same list rather than a new shallow copy.
Believing append and extend behave identically, or that append with a list spreads its elements into the target list.
Believing list.sort() returns the sorted list, when it sorts in place and returns None.
Believing lst.pop() with no argument removes the first element rather than the last.
Confusing list.remove(value), which removes by value, with pop(index), which removes by position and returns the item.
Believing zip pads shorter inputs with None, when it stops at the shortest iterable.
Believing reversed() returns a list that can be indexed, when it returns an iterator.
Believing map() and filter() return lists directly rather than lazy iterators needing list() to materialize.
Believing len() does not work on sets, when it works on all built-in sized containers.
Believing range(n) includes n, so list(range(5)) has 6 elements ending in 5.
Believing a list can be a dict key if its contents don't change; lists are unhashable regardless.
Believing 'x' in d checks a dict's values rather than its keys.
Believing membership tests on a list are O(1) like on sets and dicts, rather than O(n).
Believing dict iteration order is arbitrary in modern Python, when it follows insertion order since 3.7.
Believing split() and split(' ') behave the same, missing that split(' ') yields empty strings for adjacent spaces.
Believing string methods like replace, strip, or lower modify the string in place rather than returning a new one.
Believing int('42.5') returns 42 by truncating, when it raises ValueError.
Believing the string '0' or 'False' is falsy because of its content; any non-empty string is truthy.
Believing round() always rounds halves up as taught in school, when Python rounds half to even, so round(2.5) is 2.
Believing (1) is a one-element tuple, when the trailing comma in (1,) is what makes it a tuple.
Believing a function can assign to a module-level variable without the global keyword, or that assignment later in a function leaves earlier reads using the global.
Believing a loop's else clause runs when the loop exits via break, rather than only when it completes without break.
Believing that after an exception is caught, execution resumes inside the try block or the exception is automatically re-raised.
Believing multiple exceptions are caught with 'except A or B' or 'except A, B' rather than a tuple.

languages.label: Postgres
languages.tagline: Query planning, concurrency, and storage internals.

misconceptions.description: Believes || is logical OR (as in MySQL) rather than string concatenation in Postgres.
Believes 'a' || NULL yields 'a'; in fact concatenating with NULL yields NULL.
Confuses ILIKE with LIKE: thinks ILIKE uses regex, spans lines, or is index-friendly with a plain B-tree, rather than just being case-insensitive.
Mixes up psql meta-commands for listing objects (\dt, \dn, \l, \du, \dv, \df, \dx), e.g. thinking \dn lists tables.
Believes \c mydb creates the database or sets it as a persistent default, rather than reconnecting the session.
Believes \q commits an open transaction before exiting, rather than the transaction being rolled back.
Misreads psql toggles: thinks \x widens output or shows EXPLAIN/timing, or that \timing is something other than a per-query duration toggle.
Believes SERIAL creates a trigger, hidden counter column or identity constraint rather than a sequence with a default nextval().
Believes BIGSERIAL and SERIAL share the same integer range, when BIGSERIAL is 64-bit.
Believes inserting an explicit value into a GENERATED ALWAYS identity column succeeds or is silently overridden, rather than erroring without OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE.
Believes unquoted identifiers keep their case, rather than being folded to lowercase, and that double quotes behave like string quotes.
Believes VARCHAR(n) is measurably faster than TEXT in Postgres, when they perform essentially the same.
Believes CHAR(n) stores the value as-is or errors on shorter values, rather than padding with trailing spaces.
Believes tables created without a schema land in pg_catalog, information_schema or a 'default' schema rather than public (first on search_path).
Believes search_path controls file lookup, read permissions or databases, rather than the ordered schemas for resolving unqualified names.

Believes RETURNING on DELETE/UPDATE gives the old row for UPDATE, or misjudges what it returns (UPDATE returns new values, DELETE the deleted row); also thinks RETURNING * returns only keys or counts.
Believes ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING raises an error, upserts, or rolls back other rows, rather than silently skipping the conflicting row.
Believes the column list in ON CONFLICT (id) names columns to overwrite or index, rather than identifying the unique constraint/index to arbitrate on.
Believes Postgres arrays are 0-indexed, when they are 1-indexed by default, and misjudges slices and array_length.
Believes arrays are built with '[1,2,3]', ARRAY(1,2,3) or LIST(), rather than ARRAY[...] or the '{...}' text form.
Confuses jsonb -> (returns jsonb) with ->> (returns text), or believes they differ in nesting depth or error behavior.
Believes @> tests byte equality, key presence only, or ordering, rather than structural containment of the right value in the left.
Believes NOW() advances between calls in one transaction, when it returns the transaction start time; only clock_timestamp() changes.
Confuses return types of CURRENT_DATE (date) and NOW() (timestamptz), or related date/time functions like to_char, to_date, date_trunc and EXTRACT.
Misunderstands COALESCE (first non-NULL argument) and NULLIF (returns NULL when arguments are equal), e.g. expecting errors or zero.
Believes DISTINCT ON picks a deterministic row without a matching ORDER BY, or that it behaves like plain DISTINCT or returns only the key column.
Believes boolean columns accept bare integers or arbitrary strings like 'yes'/'maybe' without casting, or that TRUE/FALSE are case-sensitive.
Believes CHECK constraints only apply on insert, only warn, or hide failing rows, rather than being enforced on every insert and update.
Believes plain EXPLAIN runs the query and reports real runtime, when only EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes it.
Confuses pg_catalog (Postgres-specific, richer) with information_schema (SQL-standard, portable) views and their advantages.
Misreads session info functions: current_user as OS user or original login role, version() as an integer or client version, current_database() as an OID or default.
Believes :: is schema qualification, an alias or an assertion, or that CAST and :: always behave identically, rather than :: being cast shorthand.
Misunderstands INTERVAL as integer seconds or text, or thinks NOW() + INTERVAL is an error, drops time, or AGE returns an integer.
Believes generate_series or unnest return one row holding an array or a count, rather than a set of rows.
Misunderstands aggregates like string_agg and array_agg, e.g. thinking string_agg sorts, splits, or array_agg deduplicates.
Believes <> handles NULL like any value, or that IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as empty string or errors, rather than being NULL-safe comparison.
Believes nextval() values are returned on rollback or that nextval only previews, when sequence advances are non-transactional and leave gaps.
Confuses CREATE TYPE ENUM, composite types and CREATE DOMAIN with CHECK constraints, lookup tables, arrays or documentation-only aliases.
Believes wrapping an indexed column in a function or cast (lower(email), id::text, left(sku,8)) still uses its plain B-tree index, and that count(*)>0 is as cheap as EXISTS.

languages.label: JavaScript
languages.tagline: Coercion, scope, and the runtime behavior that surprises.

misconceptions.description: Believes typeof null returns "null" rather than "object", which is a long-standing quirk of the language.
Believes typeof [] returns "array" when arrays are reported as "object".
Believes NaN is not of type number, when typeof NaN is "number".
Believes typeof on an undeclared identifier throws a ReferenceError, when it safely returns "undefined".
Believes == compares without type conversion, so 1 == "1" is false, or that [] == false is false.
Believes null and undefined are indistinguishable, or that null == undefined is false while null === undefined is true.
Believes NaN === NaN is true, rather than NaN being the only value not equal to itself.
Believes global isNaN and Number.isNaN behave the same; isNaN coerces its argument first, so isNaN("foo") is true.
Believes Object.is and === always agree, missing that they differ for NaN and for +0 versus -0.
Believes decimal floating-point arithmetic is exact, so 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 is true.
Believes Number("") is NaN, when an empty string converts to 0.
Believes parseInt and Number treat trailing junk the same, so Number("10px") is 10 or parseInt("10px") is NaN.
Believes a leading zero makes parseInt("08", 10) parse as octal or give NaN or 0, rather than 8.
Believes empty arrays and empty objects are falsy, when Boolean([]) and Boolean({}) are true.
Believes the non-empty string "false" is falsy, when Boolean("false") is true.
Believes ?? falls back for any falsy value like ||, rather than only for null and undefined.
Believes || and && always return true or false instead of one of their operand values.
Believes optional chaining on null throws a TypeError rather than short-circuiting to undefined.
Believes const makes the referenced object immutable, so changing obj.a on a const object throws.
Believes reassigning a const binding silently fails or succeeds, rather than throwing a TypeError.
Believes let variables read before declaration give undefined like var, rather than a ReferenceError from the temporal dead zone.
Believes var is block scoped like let, rather than function scoped.
Believes function expressions assigned to variables are hoisted and callable before their line like function declarations.
Believes default parameters and destructuring defaults apply for null as well as undefined.
Believes arrow functions have their own arguments object or can be used with new.
Believes map mutates the original array in place instead of returning a new one.
Confuses what array methods return, such as push returning the array or element rather than the new length, or unshift returning the array.
Believes find returns an array of matches or null on failure, rather than the first match or undefined; also that findIndex returns undefined.
Believes slice mutates the original array, or that splice returns a single removed element and leaves the array unchanged.
Believes spreading an array or object makes a deep copy, so nested objects are independent of the original.
Believes sort() without a comparator sorts numbers numerically, when it compares their string forms.
Believes for...in yields array values rather than string keys, or that it excludes inherited enumerable properties.
Believes JSON.stringify keeps undefined and function-valued properties, and doesn't convert undefined array elements to null.
Believes delete on an array element removes it and shifts the others, rather than leaving a hole with the same length.
Believes the in operator checks only own properties, ignoring inherited ones such as toString.
Believes Object.keys lists all properties, including non-enumerable ones and symbol keys.
Believes Math.max accepts an array directly, or that Math.max() with no arguments returns 0 or NaN.
Believes + always does numeric addition, so '5' + 1 is 6, and that - behaves the same way as + with strings.
Believes array includes and Set has have the same lookup cost, or that reduce with spread is as efficient as map.
Believes switch compares cases with == so "1" matches 1, or that cases never fall through without break.

languages.label: Go
languages.tagline: Slices, interfaces, goroutines, and the zero values in between.

misconceptions.description: Believing map iteration follows insertion order or sorted key order, rather than being deliberately randomised.
Believing Go implicitly converts between numeric types, so int and int64 or int and float64 can be mixed in an expression without a conversion.
Believing 3/2 produces 1.5, rather than integer division truncating toward zero when both operands are integers.
Confusing T(x) conversion with x.(T) type assertion, expecting one to do the other's runtime interface check.

languages.label: Ruby
languages.tagline: Blocks, objects, and the dynamic behavior underneath.

misconceptions.description: Believing nil == false is true, or that nil and false are interchangeable values rather than distinct objects.
Believing procs and lambdas behave identically, missing that lambdas check arity strictly and return only from themselves.
Believing "a" + 1 or "5" + 5 coerces automatically, rather than raising TypeError and needing to_s or to_i.
Believing 7 / 2 yields 3.5, rather than integer division truncating toward negative infinity to give 3.
Believing ==, eql? and equal? all test the same thing, rather than value equality, type-strict equality, and object identity.
Believing === is a stricter equality operator as in JavaScript, rather than case-subsumption (class membership, regexp match, range inclusion).
Believing `and`/`or` are exact synonyms for &&/||, missing that their much lower precedence changes how assignments parse.
Believing include gives true multiple inheritance with unordered lookup, rather than inserting modules into a defined ancestor chain.
